diagnostic_evidence.quote: Then the functional $J : H^1(\Omega) \to \R$ in Definition \ref{def:cost_functional} has a unique global minimum.
establish the well-posedness of the problem, and derive the corresponding optimality system

issues.failure_explanation: The problem posed is (eq:OCP): minimise J(c(·,T;ε)) over measurable controls ε∈𝓔 subject to the nonlinear agent dynamics. Theorem thm:existence1 only proves that J has a unique minimiser over all of H^1(Ω); that minimiser is generally not reachable by the dynamics, and nothing is said about existence of an optimal control. Existence for (eq:OCP) is nontrivial: the control enters F nonlinearly through φ(r^ε), so weak-* compactness of 𝓔 does not give closedness of the reachable set without a relaxation/convexity argument. The paper (intro and Section 3) nevertheless claims well-posedness of the control problem.

failure_location.quote: The following result ensures the well-posedness of the problem

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Withdraw the well-posedness claim for (eq:OCP) and present thm:existence1 only as a property of J; alternatively state and prove existence for the time-discretised problem actually solved numerically (controls in the compact set E^M, cost continuous in the control, Weierstrass).
issues.overall_effect: The advertised well-posedness (existence of an optimal control, hence of the 'optimal trajectory') for (eq:OCP) and, by extension, for (eq:OCP_TV) is unsupported; Theorem thm:existence1 itself remains true but is about a different problem.
issues.title: Well-posedness of the optimal control problem (OCP) is claimed but only minimisation of J over H^1 is proved
issues.why_classification: A promised result (well-posedness of the control problem) must either be withdrawn or replaced by a new, though standard, existence argument in the discretised setting; the numerical method and its claims are otherwise unaffected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote:
&=\int_\Omega \lambda(x,T)\, v(x,T)\ dx -  \int_\Omega \int_0^T [- \partial_t\lambda - \partial_c F(c,\varepsilon) \cdot \lambda]\, v\ dt dx +\\
    & \hspace{7.3cm} + \int_\Omega  [-\Delta c(x,T) + \alpha (c(x,T) - I) ]\, v(x,T) dx,

issues.failure_explanation: With λ(T) = −Δc + α(c−I) and the stated adjoint equation, D = ∂_εF·λ is exactly the gradient of ε↦J(c(T;ε)), so the descent step is ε − τD, which is what the Armijo tests evaluate. The final update instead moves in the direction +D (ascent), so the step accepted by the line search is applied in the opposite direction, and the sufficient-decrease guarantee is lost. The ambiguity is not resolvable by inspection because the appendix derivation itself is sign-inconsistent: from ∫λ(T)v(T)+∫[−Δc+α(c−I)]v(T)=0 one obtains λ(T)=Δc−α(c−I), not the stated condition; with that λ the +D update would be right and the line search wrong. One of the two conventions must be chosen and the other repaired.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Fix the sign convention consistently: keep λ(T) as in eq:opt_system-b (so D = ∇J), change the update to ε^{(j+1)} ← Π_E(ε^{(j)} − σ^{(j+1)}D^{(j)}), and correct the sign in the appendix conclusion (or equivalently flip the sign of the multiplier term in eq:augmented_cost).
issues.overall_effect: Algorithm alg:dal as written is not a descent method: either the update or the line-search direction is wrong, and the appendix derivation does not yield eq:opt_system-b as stated. Algorithm alg:admm inherits the inner step.
issues.title: DAL update uses +D while the line search validates −D; terminal condition sign in the appendix derivation is inconsistent with the augmented functional
issues.why_classification: A local sign correction restores a valid projected descent method with no loss of content, though the reader must decide which of two conflicting conventions to repair.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we employ a two-way Armijo backtracking line search method \cite{A_1966} to select the best descent step-size at each iteration

issues.failure_explanation: In the ELSE branch the loop continues while the Armijo condition holds and exits at the first τ^{(k)} for which it fails; the algorithm then sets σ^{(j+1)} ← τ^{(k)}, i.e. the step actually used is one that does not satisfy the sufficient-decrease condition (the last valid step is τ^{(k-1)}). Thus the accepted step is not guaranteed to decrease J, contrary to the stated purpose of the line search.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: In the expansion branch set σ^{(j+1)} ← τ^{(k−1)} (the last step satisfying the Armijo condition).
issues.overall_effect: Monotone decrease of the cost along alg:dal iterations (and the inner step of alg:admm) is not guaranteed whenever the expansion branch is taken.
issues.title: Expansion branch of the two-way line search returns the first step that violates the Armijo condition
issues.why_classification: A one-index local correction restores the intended guarantee without changing the method.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For our purposes, we add a projection $\Pi_E$ onto the convex set $E$ to bound the control at each step.
However, when the control is constrained, the equality is not verified on the boundary of the compact set $E$.

issues.failure_explanation: The sufficient-decrease threshold c τ|D|^2 is the unconstrained Armijo bound, but the trial point is Π_E(ε − τD). When ε^{(j)} lies on ∂E and D points outward on some component (the situation Remark rmk:convergence explicitly anticipates), the projection cancels that component, so the actual decrease is of order τ|D_free|^2 while the test requires cτ|D|^2; if |D_free|^2 < c|D|^2 (e.g. D_free = 0 at a constrained stationary point) the inequality fails for every τ>0 and the backtracking WHILE loop does not terminate. The correct projected-gradient test uses ⟨D, ε − Π_E(ε−τD)⟩ in place of τ|D|^2.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the right-hand side by J(ε^{(j)}) − c⟨D^{(j)}, ε^{(j)} − Π_E(ε^{(j)} − τD^{(j)})⟩ (standard projected Armijo rule), and stop when the projected step is zero.
issues.overall_effect: alg:dal (and hence alg:admm) is not guaranteed to terminate its inner line search near active constraints, exactly where the constrained optimality conditions of rmk:convergence are expected to hold.
issues.title: Armijo test with |D|^2 is incompatible with projection: backtracking loop may never terminate at active constraints
issues.why_classification: A standard local modification of the acceptance test fixes the defect without changing method or conclusions.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: One should ensure that the compact set $E$ is large enough to allow both global interactions, i.e. $\phi(r_{ij}^\varepsilon)>0$ for any $i,j = 1,\ldots,N$
Classical results for opinion dynamics models~\cite{MotschTadmor2014} ensure that, under mild assumptions on $\phi$, the solution converges to a finite number of clusters in finite time.

issues.failure_explanation: With φ(r) = (4r−1)(1−r)^4 one has φ(0) = −1 and φ(r) < 0 for 0 ≤ r < 1/4, so the closest agents (in space and colour) repel each other and, as ε→0 (the 'global interaction' regime required in rmk:parameters), all weights become negative. This violates the positivity of the alignment kernel assumed by the cited consensus/clustering results and makes the requirement φ(r_ij^ε) > 0 for all i,j impossible. The C^2 Wendland function is (4r+1)(1−r)^4_+, but as written the model's dynamics differ qualitatively.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace (4r−1) by (4r+1) in eq:kernel (the Wendland C^2 function), which is nonnegative on [0,1].
issues.overall_effect: The kernel actually specified for all numerical tests is not a nonnegative alignment kernel; the clustering interpretation, the requirement in rmk:parameters and the connection to consensus dynamics do not hold for it as written.
issues.title: Interaction kernel as written is negative near r=0, contradicting the required positive (consensus) interactions
issues.why_classification: A single local correction restores a nonnegative kernel consistent with all surrounding claims; no argument or conclusion changes.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: There exists a saddle point for the functional $L : H^1(\Omega) \times L^2(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^2) \times L^2(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^2) \to \R$ defined in \eqref{eq:cost_tv_regular}.

issues.failure_explanation: (i) L(·,·,μ) is not coercive on H^1×L^2: along (u_n, v_n=∇u_n) with ∫|∇u_n| and ‖u_n‖_{L^2} bounded but ‖∇u_n‖_{L^2}→∞, L stays bounded, so the H^1-type coercivity of thm:existence1 does not transfer. (ii) The dual coercivity required by the Ekeland–Temam saddle-point theorem (some (u_0,v_0) with L(u_0,v_0,μ)→−∞ as ‖μ‖→∞) fails since L is linear in μ and constant along directions μ ⟂ (v_0−∇u_0). (iii) The statement itself is false in general: since max_μ L is +∞ unless v=∇u, a saddle point requires u to minimise K over H^1; for I = χ_D (a disk) the ROF minimiser is a scaled χ_D ∉ H^1, so inf_{H^1} K is not attained and no saddle point in H^1×L^2×L^2 exists.

failure_location.quote: Finally, as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:existence1}, it is immediate to show coercivity in the primal variables, ensuring that the minimum is attained in a weakly compact set. The ensemble of these properties is sufficient to guarantee the existence of a saddle point in our setting (see for instance \cite[Chapter VI]{ET_1999})

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the theorem in the finite-dimensional (pixel-discretised) setting actually used numerically, where K is coercive on R^N, the linear constraint v=∇u trivially satisfies a constraint qualification, and standard convex duality (e.g. Fenchel–Rockafellar) gives a saddle point and zero gap; or move to BV(Ω) with an appropriate dual space.
issues.overall_effect: Existence of a saddle point and the asserted strong duality (eq:duality) in the stated function spaces are not established and can fail; the claimed uniqueness of the primal minimiser in H^1 and the justification of the ADMM stopping criterion lose their formal basis.
issues.title: Saddle point theorem: coercivity claims are false and the statement fails in the H^1 setting
issues.why_classification: The proof cannot be patched locally in the H^1 setting (the statement is false there), but a comparable result holds with a contained standard argument in the discrete setting, without new global architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: However, this does not pose an issue for the numerical algorithms, which will converge to the unique primal solution and to one of the optimal dual ones.

issues.failure_explanation: A saddle point (u*,v*,μ*) must satisfy L(u*,v*,μ*) ≤ L(u,v,μ*) for all (u,v), i.e. μ* must be a Lagrange multiplier: μ* ∈ ∂|v*| pointwise and div μ* = α(u*−I). The vanishing of ∫μ·(v*−∇u*) at the primal optimum does not make an arbitrary μ optimal; e.g. μ ≡ M e_1 with M large fails the ∂|v*|-condition, and L(u,v,μ) can be driven below L(u*,v*,μ) by varying v. Dual optimal sets are non-unique only where |∇u*| = 0 (unit-ball freedom subject to the divergence constraint).

failure_location.quote: the term $\int_\Omega \mu \cdot (v^*-\nabla u^*)$ vanishes, so that any $\mu \in L^2(\Omega; \R^2)$ becomes feasible.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the sentence with the correct characterisation of dual optimal μ (μ ∈ ∂|∇u*|, div μ = α(u*−I)), noting non-uniqueness on {∇u* = 0}.
issues.overall_effect: The stated reason for non-uniqueness of the saddle point is mathematically wrong; the remark that the algorithm converges to 'one of the optimal dual ones' is not supported by this argument.
issues.title: Incorrect justification of dual non-uniqueness: not every μ is a saddle-point partner
issues.why_classification: A local rewording with the correct optimality conditions fixes the remark; nothing else depends on it.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we lose convexity in the control-to-state map $\varepsilon \mapsto c(\,\cdot\,,T; \varepsilon)$, so we can only expect convergence to a local minimum in the first variable.

until the gap between the subsequent decrease and increase in the cost functional -- given, respectively, by the minimisation in the primal variables and the maximisation in the dual one -- is small enough.

issues.failure_explanation: Theorem thm:saddle_point (even if repaired) concerns L over all u ∈ H^1. Problem (eq:OCP_TV) restricts u to the reachable set {c(·,T;ε): ε∈𝓔}, which is nonconvex by the paper's own admission. For a nonconvex primal feasible set, min_{ε,v} max_μ L = min_ε K(c(T;ε)) can strictly exceed max_μ min_{ε,v} L, so strong duality for (eq:OCP_TV) does not follow, and the ADMM stopping rule based on a vanishing primal–dual gap has no guarantee of being attainable or of certifying optimality. The paper claims the theorem ensures no duality gap for the problem solved by alg:admm.

failure_location.quote: This is the reason why Theorem \ref{thm:saddle_point} is fundamental: it ensures that there is no duality gap.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the no-gap statement to the convex problem in (u,v,μ) with u unconstrained, and state explicitly that for (eq:OCP_TV) the gap-based stopping rule is heuristic and only local stationarity in ε can be expected.
issues.overall_effect: The theoretical justification of the ADMM stopping criterion and of the saddle-point interpretation of alg:admm for (eq:OCP_TV) is unsupported; alg:admm remains a heuristic for the nonconvex control problem.
issues.title: No-duality-gap claim for the nonconvex control problem (OCP_TV) is not implied by Theorem saddle_point
issues.why_classification: A stated guarantee (zero duality gap, hence a certified stopping criterion) must be withdrawn for the actual control problem; the algorithm survives as a heuristic, so the loss is limited but more than cosmetic.
